rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.7, 3.2, Table 2 - the authors built a float-sensor/RF/microcontroller pump controller and field-tested it in Kharif 2018-19 at CIAE Bhopal, measuring pump discharge with a water meter and recording yield. Q2: Abstract, Section 3.2, Table 2 - the automated sensor-based system (AWD mode) gave irrigation water productivity 6.15 vs 3.06 kg/ha/mm and total water savings of 36% compared with the control under continuous ponding. Q7: Sections 2.6 and 3.2 (discussion) - the field must be laser-levelled before installation for smooth water flow; the system requires a reliable power source; the pump house must lie within the 100 m RF range of the field sensor; larger fields need multiple sensors/valves; farmers may need training. Q8: Section 3.2 discussion and Conclusions - authors list limitations (designed only for rice under AWD, power dependence, 100 m range, cost/complexity for larger fields) and state the study mainly compares AWD with continuous ponding, focusing on development and water saving rather than the system's specific crop effects.
rows.notes: The 36% saving is confounded: the automated plot used AWD while the control used continuous ponding, so the saving cannot be attributed to automation alone (authors themselves say the study primarily compares AWD and CP). Single season, single plot pair, one site, one cultivar. Water use measured by one method (mechanical water meter), no second method. Seasonal water-level or percolation data not reported, only sensor calibration (R2 0.99). Yield has SD (4.8<U+00B1>0.189 vs 4.1/4.2<U+00B1>0.429 t/ha, inconsistent between text and table) but no dispersion for water saving or water productivity. The technology label 'app_scheduling' fits loosely: the system is a sensor-controller automation without an app, but it matches the review's definition of smart irrigation.

notes: Full text available; some pages duplicated/garbled by layout overlap but content legible. Yield for control is given as 4.2 t/ha in text and 4.1 t/ha in Table 2.
